issues.title: The absolute pairing fails to preserve direct sums
issues.location: Section 4.3, Proposition 4.3 (Whittaker duality), immediately after Equation (4.3)
issues.classification_note: A continuous evaluation for the full parameter class remains to be constructed. The counterexample tests the stated generality at s = 0; it is not a counterexample at irrational level.

feedback.text: The absolute pairing (W2) is not continuous for the full stated parameter class. Take S to be a countable disjoint union of points with constant marking, H = SL_2, X = P^1, and s = 0. The zero-label stratum is A^1, and the normalized pairing of opposite exponential objects is C. Let W carry the positive object on every component and V_n the negative object only on component n. All lie in the zero-pole bound, but ordinary global sections give B(W,⊕_n V_n) = ∏_n C, while ⊕_n B(W,V_n) = ⊕_n C. Neither the bounded-zero convention nor increasing pole bounds removes this failure. This counterexample does not challenge the pairing on X^I or the relative pairing.

For the stated non-quasi-compact parameter generality, distinguish ordinary absolute de Rham sections from a continuous categorical evaluation and justify the construction supporting the asserted duality. Check agreement with (W2) on quasi-compact parameters and compatibility with the claimed closed-image transposition identities. In the disjoint-union example, continuity requires the direct sum of the componentwise evaluations; that observation alone does not construct the evaluation for general S. The current extension in pole bounds does not supply this parameter-direction argument.

issues.title: Constant fibres do not imply a global scalar identification
issues.location: Section 6.1, proof of Proposition 6.1, final paragraph of the diagonal calculation
issues.classification_note: The report supplies a local-trivialization and descent repair that preserves the required conservativity without a global splitting.

feedback.text: The global scalar-identity assertion at lines 3299–3300 is too strong. After the stated cancellations, the diagonal coefficient is E=p_*ω_{H×N}, where p(h',n)=h'B⁻ after the change h'=hn, up to fixed normalization shifts. For H=SL₂, its ordinary constant-sheaf counterpart is Rπ_*ℂ_{SL₂} on P¹. A constant derived coefficient with fibre H*(B⁻) would have four-dimensional total global cohomology, whereas the actual pushforward has H*(SL₂), of total dimension two. Thus constant fibre cohomology does not eliminate the torsor's derived extension data. This disproves the global scalar identification, not the required conservativity.

Replace the global scalar-identity conclusion at lines 3299–3300 with a justification of conservativity using the actual diagonal coefficient. Retain the proposition's scope of all twisted D-modules and spectator factors, since that conservativity is used at lines 3884–3885.

Keep E=p_*ω_{H×N}, with p(h',n)=h'B⁻. Trivialize H→H/B⁻ on translates of the big cell. On each covering open U, the coefficient becomes ω_U⊗V, where V=Γ_dR(B⁻×N,ω) is a nonzero finite complex. Over ℂ, V splits into shifted finite-dimensional vector spaces, so tensoring with V detects zero for arbitrary input complexes. Descent therefore makes tensoring with E conservative globally. The same calculation on products with spectator charts preserves spectators. Together with the preceding diagonal-support calculation, this proves conservativity of the composite and hence of finite averaging, supplying the conservativity needed downstream without asserting a global splitting.

social.claim: The global scalar-identity assertion in the finite-averaging argument is too strong: constant fibre cohomology does not eliminate a torsor’s derived extension data.
evidence: After the stated cancellations, the diagonal coefficient is E = p_*ω_{H×N}, where p(h′, n) = h′B⁻, up to fixed normalization shifts. For H = SL₂, the constant-sheaf counterpart is Rπ_*ℂ_{SL₂} on ℙ¹ for π : SL₂ → ℙ¹. Here B⁻ is the opposite Borel subgroup and N the unipotent subgroup in the averaging construction.

With complex coefficients and dimensions summed over all degrees, a constant derived coefficient with fibre H*(B⁻) would give total dimension four. The actual pushforward instead has the cohomology of SL₂, of total dimension two:
social.conclusion: The claimed global scalar identification fails. The report proposes a repair of conservativity using the actual coefficient and descent.

title: A power saving for planar unit distances
summary: Genericity over a coefficient field can be lost after adjoining another grid point.

issues.title: Genericity can fail after enlarging the coefficient field
issues.location: Section 8.2, final sentence of the function-field discussion after the proof of Lemma 8.3
issues.classification_note: The proposed correction narrows the original assertion. The report explains why the cited applications are preserved, but does not establish the broader assertion as written.
issues.expert_comment: The reported issue and the suggested fix are both correct. So the statement in the paper is false as stated, but this error is fixable.

feedback.text: The automatic enlargement assertion at lines 3507–3509 is too broad. For grid vertices p,r, put a=z_p, b=z_r and B=B_0(a+b). The generic-grid lemma implies that p is generic over B, but adjoining r makes a belong to B(r), reducing p’s transcendence degree below its locus dimension. Thus joint genericity over B_0 does not justify adjoining other grid points to arbitrary B. The preceding evaluation criterion, which explicitly assumes genericity over its coefficient field, is unaffected.
Revise lines 3507–3509 to distinguish genericity guaranteed by the generic-grid lemma from genericity that must be established over a larger coefficient field.

Restrict automatic preservation to adjoining other grid points to B_0. Their selected coordinates are jointly independent of the point’s selected coordinates, and adjoining their remaining curve coordinates is algebraic, so the point remains generic. For an arbitrary larger coefficient field, retain the explicit genericity hypothesis. The application over K_0 already establishes that hypothesis separately at lines 3600–3612; the later anchor applications use independence over B_0 and algebraic extensions. This correction resolves the identified overstatement without changing those arguments.

social.claim: At the end of Section 8.2, the paper asserts that a point generic over a coefficient field stays generic after adjoining other grid points. The grid lemma guarantees joint independence over the base field B₀, but not over an arbitrary larger field.
evidence: Let p and r be distinct grid vertices, with p on a curve or plane V over B₀ of dimension d ∈ {1, 2}. The selected coordinates are jointly algebraically independent over B₀; each vertex’s remaining coordinates are algebraic over B₀ and its own selected coordinates.
Choose selected coordinates a of p and b of r, and set B = B₀(a + b). Since b is transcendental over B₀(p), the point p remains generic over B, with transcendence degree d. But adjoining r gives:
equations: trdeg over B(r) of B(r, p) ≤ d − 1
social.conclusion: One of p’s independent coordinates is now in the coefficient field. Thus p is no longer generic on V over B(r). The evaluation criterion that explicitly assumes genericity is unaffected.

PRE refinement of CURRENT supplies the first condition at every event, and the linked-event inclusion supplies the second. This endpoint correction requires no change to the chain-length bound used in the linear-side energy argument.

issues.title: The predictor identity omits a conditional-expectation term
issues.location: Section 5.2, proof of Lemma 5.3, predictor-moment identity and its increment
issues.classification_note: The supplied correction preserves the parameter dependence of estimate (7), with adjusted absolute constants.

feedback.text: The predictor identity at lines 2708–2715 omits a term for the general augmented inputs admitted in this section. Orthogonality gives μ_h=εa_{h,p}−√ε E_h[(F_a)_p], so its increment also includes −√ε(E_{h+1}−E_h)[(F_a)_p]. For example, F_a=Φ_p has zero residual and predictor coefficient one, contradicting μ_h=εa_{h,p}. The stated identity is valid for scalar embeddings, and this counterexample does not disprove estimate (7).

Correct the predictor-moment identity and its increment for the stated augmented-input domain, and carry the additional conditional-expectation term through the smooth-bump, coarse-mean, and curvature-difference estimates in the proof of (7).

Set f_p=(F_a)_p and use μ_h=√ε[(P_hF_a)_p−E_hf_p]. The projection increments and conditional-expectation increments each have a sum of squared L²(J) norms at most ||F_a||²₂. Consequently (∑_h||μ_{h+1}−μ_h||²₂)^(1/2)≤2√ε||F_a||₂ and ||μ_H||₂≤2√ε||F_a||₂. In the existing proof, these bounds retain the 2^(−K_0), K_0√ε, and √ε contributions with adjusted absolute constants. Thus this correction preserves the parameter dependence needed for (7) and its high-truncation application; for scalar embeddings the added term vanishes.

issues.title: The first-failing-role convention uses the wrong order

feedback.text: Lines 6789–6793 contain a local convention mismatch. Assignment to the first failing role requires each role to succeed at trials assigned to later roles. Requiring success at trials assigned to earlier roles instead describes assignment to the last failing role. Both conventions partition failed trials, so this mismatch does not itself invalidate the subsequent summed estimates.

Keep the first-failing-role convention and replace “the earlier roles' required positions” with “the trials assigned to later roles.” Explicitly, if a(t) is the assigned role, role j must fail when a(t)=j and succeed when a(t)>j, with no condition when a(t)<j. Retain success in every core role at the final height. These corrected masks still select whole minimal-component core subtotals by predicate coherence. For each fixed assignment, the assigned failure counts n_j remain unchanged, and the upper bounds at lines 7052–7071 still follow by discarding the additional success conditions.

feedback.text: The unqualified C/d(s) integral estimate in lines 2493–2494 is too strong for the full second kernel R(s,v)=θ′(s)θ′(v)/sin²((θ(s)+θ(v))/2). The endpoint estimate is valid locally, but a global estimate needs a bounded bulk contribution.
Qualify C/d(s) as an endpoint-region estimate and account separately for the bounded bulk contribution, or replace the full-kernel integral bound by C(1+1/d(s)).

The exact integral 4θ′(s)/sinθ(s), together with θ′=πλ_L and sinθ(s) comparable to λ_L(s)min(1,d(s)), gives the corrected global bound C(1+1/d(s)). By symmetry of R, this yields ∫∫R(s,v)|Q(s)+Q(v)|²dsdv≤C(‖Q‖₂²+∫_{d(s)≤2}|Q(s)|²/d(s)ds). Thus the existing L² term absorbs the bulk contribution, preserving the upper comparison in line 2478 and its use in the subsequent gap and counting argument.

These changes correct the references to the intended inputs; they do not replace the candidate's separate arguments extending the fixed-level constructions.

issues.title: A cited finiteness result is described as boundedness
issues.classification_note: Terminology. Section 6 deduces Corollary 1.2 from the finiteness statement of [11], so the corollary and its proof are unaffected.

feedback.text: The unqualified “boundedness” description in lines 128–130 is imprecise. EFGMS Theorem B gives finiteness of locally trivial deformation classes in fixed dimension, while its following paragraph explicitly distinguishes this from forming a bounded family. Your later formulation in lines 2626–2636 uses the needed finiteness conclusion, so this is a terminology issue. See [EFGMS v1, page 3 and Definition 2.25](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.00973v1).

In lines 128–129, replace “the boundedness of Lagrangian-fibered symplectic varieties” with “the finiteness, in each fixed dimension, of locally trivial deformation classes represented by primitive symplectic varieties admitting a Lagrangian fibration”. This matches the cited conclusion and the finiteness argument already given in lines 2626–2636.
